sections.html:
Indianapolis is the Indiana capital and the seat of Marion County, a consolidated city-county whose limits match the county except for four separate towns and cities: Beech Grove, Lawrence, Southport and Speedway. Nine civil townships divide the county: Center, Decatur, Franklin, Lawrence, Perry, Pike, Warren, Washington and Wayne. A house in Perry Township or Pike Township is in a real map location with its own schools, fire and assessor boundaries.

The 2020 count was 887,642 residents. The median owner-occupied home value is $224,800, and 56.0% of households own their homes, which means nearly half rent. That matters if your house has tenants. These are citywide medians, and a home in a historic district and a house on a street with several vacant lots can sit far from them, so treat the numbers as context and not as a price for your property.

Large employers such as Eli Lilly, Amazon and FedEx shape housing demand, and an owner facing a transfer or relocation may want a sale on a set date.

Indianapolis was a planned city, laid out in 1821 as a one-mile-square grid around a central circle. Housing followed the transit lines, and the streetcar suburbs include Broad Ripple, Irvington and University Heights. The city has 13 local historic districts and five conservation areas, among them Chatham-Arch, Fountain Square, Lockerbie Square, Old Northside, Irvington and Woodruff Place.

Age shows up in the details a buyer prices in:

  • Original knob-and-tube wiring or older panels in pre-war homes.
  • Clay or cast iron sewer laterals under mature trees.
  • Brick foundations, wet basements and old plaster.
  • Exterior changes in a historic district that may need review before work starts.

The city counts roughly 500 registered neighborhood associations, so an association may also have rules about exterior work or signs.

Indianapolis has hot summers, cold winters and rain in every month, with 42.4 inches of rain and 25.9 inches of snow in a typical year. The record high is 106 degrees and the record low is minus 27. That swing is hard on roofs, gutters, driveways and HVAC equipment.

The White River runs 31 miles through the city and is fed by about 35 streams, including Eagle Creek, Fall Creek, Pleasant Run and Pogue's Run. Homes near those waterways may sit in mapped flood zones, and a lender may require flood insurance. Check the parcel on FEMA's flood map service before you list.

  • Check the gutters and grading if a basement has ever taken water.
  • Keep receipts for roof or drainage work, since buyers ask.
  • Photograph any storm damage before repairs.

sections.h2: Rentals, short-term rentals and vacant houses
sections.html:
Owners of residential rental units must register them, and the Department of Business and Neighborhood Services (DBNS) runs the registry. If you are selling a rented house, the lease, the registry record and any open code issues all become part of the sale conversation.

Short-term rentals have their own permit program, in effect since January 1, 2025, with a one-time $150 fee for the first permit and no fee for renewals. The unit must be a legally built dwelling that meets applicable building code.

Vacant houses face the Continuous Vacancy program, which began January 1, 2026 and targets homes that have gone six years without improvement. Repair orders can last up to two years, and negligent owners can be fined up to $5,000 per year, with fines adjusted if the owner works with DBNS. If you inherited a vacant Indianapolis house, call DBNS before the problem grows.

Before the Marion County Recorder will record a deed, the Assessor's Office has to stamp it. Have your title company, attorney or another preparer draw up the deed itself. Filing can be done by mail, through e-recording partners or in person. Your title company can estimate how long recording will take after closing.

Indiana transfers also carry a sales disclosure form under IC 6-1.1-5.5-3. Buyer and seller complete it, the county assessor reviews it, and the county auditor files it ahead of the conveyance document.

  • Ask for a payoff letter if any mortgage or lien is on the house.
  • Gather landlord registry details if the house is rented.
  • Confirm any open code orders with DBNS.

Indianapolis owners pay property tax in two installments, May 10 and November 10. Whichever falls close to your sale date gets prorated by the closing agent, and tax still owed comes out of your proceeds at closing. Call the county treasurer if you want today's balance before you accept an offer.

Owners who live in the house may benefit from the state homestead deduction, which is the lesser of $45,000 or 60% of gross assessed value. Ask the county auditor how it applies to your bill.

sections.h2: Steps from first call to closing
sections.html:
1. Give us the address, the condition of the house and whether anyone lives there.
  2. We look at the property and make an offer.
  3. If you accept, the title company searches the deed for liens, unpaid taxes and open code orders.
  4. You sign the deed and the sales disclosure form.
  5. The Assessor's Office stamps the deed, the Recorder records it, and you are paid.

Delays usually come from the title search. A payoff letter, a stale registry record or a code order nobody has closed can each add days. Mention them early.

Sellers who want speed usually fit one of a few patterns, and the pattern sets the pace of the sale.

  • An inherited house that needs probate, clean-out or repairs.
  • A rental with a tenant, postponed maintenance or a registry question.
  • A vacant house that has drawn code attention.
  • An older home with plumbing, electrical or foundation trouble.
  • A job move that leaves a mortgage and an empty house behind.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works here
sections.html:
We buy Indianapolis houses as-is. Tell us about the house and any tenants and we make an offer. Once you accept, a title company searches the deed, prepares the disclosure form and sets the closing date. Cash can sidestep lender appraisals and repair demands, though a normal listing deserves a side-by-side comparison.

Get the offer in writing, find out who pays for title and recording, and read the contract before signing. On the first call, have your tax bill, payoff figures and any lease close at hand.

An inherited house in Indianapolis may need probate before a deed can be prepared, and it may also need a clean-out. Heirs often live elsewhere and carry the utilities, insurance and tax bill while the house sits. If the property is empty, check with DBNS about vacancy rules before the problem grows. Collect the estate papers, the tax bill and the keys before you talk to a buyer or the title company, and ask what the deed needs.

faqs.q: Do I have to register a rental house in Indianapolis before selling?
faqs.a: Owners of residential rental units in Indianapolis are required to register them with the city. If the house is currently rented, make sure the registry record is current so the sale paperwork lines up.

faqs.q: How long does recording a deed take in Marion County?
faqs.a: The deed must first be stamped by the Assessor's Office in Room W121, then submitted by mail, e-recording or in person. Your title company can tell you the timing for your closing.

faqs.q: Does Indianapolis have a short-term rental permit?
faqs.a: Yes. A permit program began January 1, 2025, with a one-time $150 fee for the first permit and no renewal fee. The unit must be a legally built dwelling that meets applicable building code.

faqs.q: What is the Continuous Vacancy program?
faqs.a: It is a DBNS program that began January 1, 2026 for vacant homes that have gone six years without improvement. Repair orders can run up to two years, and fines can reach $5,000 per year.

faqs.q: Can I sell an Indianapolis house that needs major repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. You can sell it as is, though a lender-financed buyer may require repairs. A cash buyer can buy without those requirements, so compare the written terms before choosing.
